discovery: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation, including topological (surface) codes
subfield: Quantum information physics / quantum error correction
motivation: Quantum superpositions were long believed too fragile to protect, since measurement destroys them and the no-cloning theorem forbids copying them. Shor (1995) and Steane (1996) independently found that quantum information can be encoded redundantly in entangled states, so that errors can be detected and corrected without learning the encoded state. Kitaev's toric code (1997) linked error correction to topological order in many-body physics. It led to the surface code, whose local stabilizers and high threshold make fault tolerance practical. Together with threshold theorems, these ideas show that arbitrarily long quantum computations are possible with imperfect hardware. In recent years, superconducting-circuit, trapped-ion and neutral-atom experiments have realized repeated stabilizer measurements and logical qubits whose errors fall as code distance grows. This confirms that the predicted regime is physically real. Quantum error correction is now the organizing principle of quantum technology and a new way of understanding protected quantum matter.
